text.p: European mediation in the Middle East made a breakthrough in Malta on Wednesday when the Europeans brought together Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country is current president of the European Union, took Levy up to see Arafat at a Valletta hotel after two days of wrangling over Palestinian conditions for such a meeting.
Arafat spokesman Marwan Kanafani described it as a courtesy call on Arafat but added that the Israeli minister had 20 minutes separately with Palestinian Planning Minister Nabil Shaath.

Neither side said the meetings made progress on substance and they set no timetable for resuming the peace talks which collapsed when Israel started building a Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem last month.

"There was a cordial and very warm exchange of ideas and recommitments to the peace process. No substance was discussed except that both leaders agreed that there should be a real attempt to go back to the peace process," Kanafani added.

"We consider this as a positive step, as a good goodwill step and hopefully we will take it from there and with the help of the European Union go ahead and start to put the peace process back on the right track," he said.
Levy, speaking in Hebrew through an interpreter, said he found the Palestinians willing to speed up talks on "final status" questions -- Jerusalem, borders and refugees.

He echoed Kanafani's assessment of the mood. "The atmosphere was a good one... There are still differences as far as positions are concerned but there is a will and a wish to resolve them through dialogue," he said.
"We will continue our efforts when we return home to define the parameters for a return to negotiations," he added.
Shaath, asked if a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would now be possible, said: "Not at this stage. This is just the beginning."
The meetings were at the highest level since Netanyahu decided last month to go ahead with the Jewish settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim or Har Homa in East Jerusalem.
Since then Palestinians have clashed daily with Israeli troops in the West Bank and the Palestinians have called off their security cooperation with the Israeli authorities.

Levy again defended the settlement on Wednesday and French Foreign Ministry spokesman said the Israeli minister told Arafat that Israel was willing to build thousands of houses for non-Jews, alongside the 6,500 planned for Har Homa.
The direct talks in Malta were a surprise twist to roller- coaster Middle East diplomacy at a conference of foreign ministers from 27 European and Mediterranean ministers.

They also gave an unexpected shot in the arm to Europe's attempts to find a role in the Middle East peace process, alongside or in friendly competition with the United States, the traditional go-between.
U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross arrives back in the region on Wednesday on a mission to put Israeli-Palestinian talks back on track after the setbacks of the last month.
The meetings took place on the sidelines of a conference called to keep alive and promote a European-Mediterranean dialogue launched in Barcelona in 1995.

The Europeans had hoped to keep the Arab-Israeli dispute in the background and concentrate on an agenda of economic, security and cultural cooperation between the northern and southern shores of the Mediterranean.
The two-day conference was meant to end by lunchtime on Wednesday but the Middle East conflict again intruded.

The French spokesman said the Dutch presidency came close to abandoning efforts to draft a consensus text on the Middle East for the final statement of the conference but later agreed that senior officials should work overtime to agree one.

The Europeans would be happy with a text which repeats what they said in Barcelona in 1995. That text specifies that a settlement should be based on the principle of land for peace -- a principle Netanyahu's rightwing government has questioned.
Delegates said both Israel and the Arabs had their own ideas about what the conference should say and that the senior officials were trying to find a compromise.
The Arabs have asked for a reference to Israel's settlement policies, seen in the Arab world as a violation of international law and of agreements reached in peace talks.

"The problem in particular is the way the document will describe the present state of the peace process. Arab states would like to add a statement that there is a stalemate in the process," Doutriaux said.

The French spokesman, whose minister took part in the Israeli-Palestinian discussions, said Arafat told Levy the Palestinians were willing to fight political violence but also brought up the Jewish settlement in Har Homa.
